parsed.explanation: The unit responds to a clearly visible, upright, roughly frontal dog face, with eyes and muzzle both in view, regardless of breed, coat colour or fur texture.
parsed.evidence: Within the top dog classes, the answers on face visibility, frontal pose, upright orientation and eyes-plus-muzzle visibility all separate activity strongly (separation at the 98th–99th percentile, d about ±0.9–1.4), while coat colour and fur texture explain almost nothing (42nd–49th percentile). Activity also peaks when the face takes up a moderate portion of the frame rather than a close-up, which fits a face-sized detector.
parsed.missing_data: Activity on photos without dog faces, such as cat, fox or human faces, or dog bodies with no face visible, which would show whether the unit is dog-specific or responds to frontal mammal faces in general.

null_s3.explanation: The unit responds to dog faces, most strongly when the face is large in the frame and the head is tilted sideways or turned to a three-quarter view, rather than upright and head-on.

parsed.explanation: The unit responds to dog faces, most strongly when the face is large in the frame and the head is tilted sideways or turned to a three-quarter view, rather than upright and head-on.
parsed.evidence: Within the top dog classes, tilted heads (d +0.64, 97th percentile), three-quarter views (d +0.26) and close-ups (d +0.38) drive activity up, while upright (d -0.55, 3rd percentile), frontal (d -0.22) and small faces (d -0.35) push it down, which contradicts the original 'upright, frontal' description. Coat colour and fur texture separate the photos only weakly, so the unit appears to generalize across breeds.
parsed.missing_data: Photos with no dog face (other animals' faces, human faces, rotated non-face objects) to test whether the unit is specific to dog faces or responds to tilted, face-like or rotated structure more generally; every photo checked here contained a dog face.
